subjective.question: Define community and community journalism.
subjective.answer: A community is a social group of organisms sharing an environment, normally with shared interests. In human communities, intent, belief, resources, preferences, needs and risks may be present in common, affecting the identity of the participants and their degree of cohesiveness. Community journalism (also called civic or public journalism) is a people-centered approach to journalism: it is the type of journalism that focuses on issues that are important to the majority of the community, connects to the local community, involves readers and community members in the process of news production, and works to build a better understanding between the community and the local media.

subjective.question: Stamm and Fortini-Campbell discuss community into three domains. Explain these three domains of community in terms of the connections or ties between people and places.
subjective.answer: Stamm and Fortini-Campbell discuss community in terms of three domains: (1) Place - a geographic territory that people can identify as their own and about which they can exercise power and authority. The place domain is about ties between people and place; it is the notion of being attached to a place, as when you look for your community's name in the newspaper to see what is being said about where you live. (2) Social structure - the ties that connect people to one another; a social structure is a group of people sharing an interest, an association of people in a common relationship or activity. (3) Social process - the ties through which people live their lives, the social actions that occur repeatedly in a place and that connect people with one another. Community is therefore a process through which people live their lives, not merely a place or a collection of people.

subjective.question: Why is it important for the journalist to become a member of the community he is working for?
subjective.answer: A community journalist has to know his community. It is important that he becomes a member of the community he is working for, because this is the way to get to know people and to understand their way of thinking. He should talk to people informally and ask about the community he covers; this is how he becomes aware of what people are thinking about, talking about and worried about. A steady stream of good ideas has always been the lifeblood of journalism, and these ideas come through knowing people, being involved with them and being around them.

subjective.question: Discuss the skills and qualities required of a community journalist.
subjective.answer: A community journalist needs practical and technical competence, compassion, common sense, responsibility, independence, involvement, initiative, integrity, performance and a people-centered approach. Probably the two most important qualities are common sense and understanding people. The journalist must become involved in the community he covers, know people and understand their way of thinking, and talk to them informally. He cannot be the lapdog of special interests, and he must not become a community insider to the extent that he becomes a special-interest reporter. To be a community journalist, one also has to be a generalist who knows a little bit about everything, rather than a specialist who knows a great deal about one thing.

subjective.question: What is public listening? How can community journalists collect information and feedback from the community?
subjective.answer: Public listening is the first step in a journalist's research of an issue; it is the way community journalists discover what topics people are thinking and talking about. Journalists can collect information and feedback from the community by: using the phone (calling a range of people when starting research on an issue); conducting in-person interviews (for stories, but also simply to get to know people); holding newsroom conversations (identifying the questions and answers that are already in the newsroom); reviewing letters to the editor (letters as an indicator of what is important to the community); and developing and fostering public forums (town meetings or similar gatherings where community journalists are on hand to listen).

subjective.question: Describe the five layers of the 'public' that community journalists must understand.
subjective.answer: The public can be segmented into five basic groups or places: (1) The official group - people who are part of the political system or recognized leaders of institutions. (2) The quasi-official group - everyday leaders to whom citizens look as quasi-officials or opinion leaders; talking to them is like talking to interview catalysts. (3) Third places - places where people gather informally, such as churches, community events and schools. (4) Incidental places - places where people come together in passing. (5) Private places - where people are at home and in their private lives. Traditional journalism goes to the first group and then to the last; community journalists focus on the middle three groups who make up the community.

subjective.question: How does community journalism differ from traditional journalism in gathering story information?
subjective.answer: To get their story information, traditional journalism tends to approach the official group first (the people in the political system or the recognized leaders of institutions) and then go to the private places where people are at home and in their private lives. Community journalism, in contrast, focuses on the middle three layers of the public - the quasi-official group of everyday leaders and opinion leaders, the third places where people gather informally, and the incidental places. It uses public listening as the first step of research, so that the issues covered are the ones that are important to the majority of the community rather than only those defined by officials.

subjective.question: What are the characteristics of the relationships between journalists, the community and the media in community journalism?
subjective.answer: In community journalism, journalists are not merely observers but are involved in the community. The media is a forum for the community, not a problem solver. Journalists, community members and the media share responsibility for making democracy work at the grassroots level. Newspapers and other media should use their resources to build connections between journalists and community members, build communities of interest within the circulation area, and create connections between community members themselves. Once an issue is chosen, the people drive the agenda, and the newspaper follows with articles that show people deliberating about the issue.

subjective.question: What is public judgment? How does deliberative discourse help in community journalism?
subjective.answer: Public judgment is the state of public opinion that arises when people have worked through an issue - considering its consequences, costs and trade-offs - rather than merely holding a top-of-the-head reaction. Deliberative discourse means dialogue, that is, lengthy discussion of issues within the community. It helps because conversation that leads to discussion brings people to a better understanding of the issue; when discussion is good, it may be that only a small number of people are talking, but everyone is listening. This dialogue helps the community weigh its options and reach sound public judgment, and it helps journalists report issues in the way citizens themselves experience them.

subjective.topic: Theories of Communication and Community Journalism
subjective.question: Discuss the role of the social responsibility theory and the Hutchins Commission in the development of community journalism.
subjective.answer: Community journalism derives many of its philosophical foundations from social responsibility theory and agenda-setting theory. Social responsibility theory holds that the press has a social responsibility to its community. The Commission on Freedom of the Press (the Hutchins Commission), set up in 1942, presented its report in 1947, laying out a code of social responsibility with five basic services required of the press: (1) a truthful, comprehensive and intelligent account of the day's events in a context which gives them meaning; (2) a forum for the exchange of comment and criticism; (3) the projection of a representative picture of the constituent groups in society; (4) the presentation and clarification of the goals and values of society; and (5) full access to the day's intelligence. These principles - informing citizens, providing a forum and clarifying society's goals and values - are the philosophical basis on which community journalism stands.

subjective.topic: Theories of Communication and Community Journalism
subjective.question: Write any three postulates of the code of social responsibility for the press suggested in the Hutchins Commission report.
subjective.answer: Any three of the following five services required of the press under the Hutchins Commission's code of social responsibility: (1) A truthful, comprehensive and intelligent account of the day's events in a context which gives them meaning. (2) A forum for the exchange of comment and criticism. (3) The projection of a representative picture of the constituent groups in society. (4) The presentation and clarification of the goals and values of society. (5) Full access to the day's intelligence.

subjective.topic: Theories of Communication and Community Journalism
subjective.question: What is development media theory? Discuss its main goals.
subjective.answer: Development media theory is part of the normative theories of the press and is closely related to community journalism. It holds that media and government share responsibility for national development. Its main goals are: (1) media must accept and carry out positive development tasks in line with nationally established policy; (2) freedom of the media should be open to restriction according to economic priorities and the development needs of society; (3) media should give priority in their content to the national culture and language; (4) media should give priority in news and information to links with other developing countries which are close geographically, culturally or politically; (5) journalists and other media workers have responsibilities as well as freedoms in their information gathering and dissemination tasks; and (6) in the interest of development ends, the state has the right to intervene in, or restrict, media operation, and devices of censorship, subsidy and direct control can be justified. Journalists should assist the government in implementing development policies rather than picking them apart.

subjective.topic: Theories of Communication and Community Journalism
subjective.question: Explain the main features of democratic-participant theory.
subjective.answer: Democratic-participant theory was proposed in recognition of new media developments and increasing criticism of the dominance of the main mass media by private or public monopolies. From the 1960s onwards, calls were heard for alternative, grass-roots media expressing the needs of citizens. The theory supports the right to relevant local information, the right to answer back, and the right to use the new means of communication for interaction and social action in small-scale settings of community, interest groups or subculture. It challenges the necessity and desirability of uniform, centralized, high-cost, commercialized, professionalized or state-controlled media; in their place it encourages multiple, small-scale, local, non-institutional and committed media that link senders to receivers and favour horizontal patterns of interaction. Participation and interaction are its key concepts, and it advocates media support for cultural pluralism at the grass-roots level.

subjective.question: Define community media. What are its major functions?
subjective.answer: According to the IAMCR, community media originates, circulates and resonates from the sphere of civil society. It is an alternative medium to mainstream state and market media and, being community owned and driven, provides an essential communicative democratic process. Community media is small-scale media owned and operated by citizens on a non-profit basis, exclusively to serve the public interest of a relatively small community. Its major functions include: providing local news and information relevant to community needs; involving and engaging members of the community in public communication; empowering the politically disenfranchised; giving voice to those without voices; preserving and promoting local culture and language; and encouraging expression and participation by the audience.

subjective.question: Write down the distinguishing characteristics of a community radio purposed by Jankowski.
subjective.answer: According to Jankowski (2001), the distinguishing characteristics of community media, including community radio, are: (1) Objectives - community radio is primarily concerned with news and information relevant to community needs, engaging members of the community in public communication, and empowering the politically disenfranchised. (2) Ownership and control - ownership and control are shared by residents, local government and community-based organizations. (3) Content - content is locally oriented and produced, dealing with matters of concern to the community. (4) Audience - the audience is predominantly the residents of a small, clearly defined geographic region. (5) Financing - financing is essentially non-commercial in nature, so the station serves the community rather than advertisers.

subjective.question: What is community radio? Discuss the two philosophical approaches to community radio.
subjective.answer: Community radio is radio made to serve people; radio that encourages expression and participation and that values local culture - in the words of Bruce Girard, founder of AMACR, it is radio that adapts itself to the tastes and needs of the community, that seeks the participation of the community and that gives voice to those without voices. Philosophically, there are two distinct approaches to community radio. The first approach stresses the notion of serving the community or being community-minded in its broadcasting. The second approach stresses involvement and participation in the medium by the listener. Both approaches are valid and, in the best community radio, are mutually reinforcing; they derive from differing traditions of political change but do not compete.

subjective.question: Discuss community radio in India, with reference to Anna FM and the Community Radio Policy of 2006.
subjective.answer: In India, the airwaves were freed by a Supreme Court judgment of 1995 which declared that airwaves are public property. Anna FM, launched on 1 February 2004 and run by the Education and Multimedia Research Centre (EM2RC) of Anna University, is India's first campus community radio; it broadcasts within a radius of about 15 km and runs programmes for the uneducated sections of the nearby community. The Community Radio Policy announced on 16 November 2006 allows non-profit organizations, civil society and voluntary organizations, state agriculture universities, ICAR institutions, Krishi Vigyan Kendras and registered societies to apply for licences. Stations use a 100 watt ERP transmitter covering about 12 km; they must produce at least 50 percent of their programming locally, preferably in the local language or dialect; advertising is limited to 5 minutes per hour, and news programmes are banned on community radio.

subjective.question: Discuss the need for and prospects of community radio in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: In Pakistan there is a dire need for community radio. The state-run PBC and PTV do not cater to the needs of far-flung communities in the local languages, and commercial FM stations are confined to the big cities, so the problems of the local population are not addressed and their voices are not heard. PEMRA, the regulatory authority, has so far issued only a handful of community radio licences, mostly to universities and NGOs. Community radio is important for remote areas like Northern Pakistan, where literacy is low and people depend on radio as their only medium of communication; it is also important for the rural population engaged in agriculture, which needs information about weather, crops and pesticides. Given this need, PEMRA should issue community radio licences generously, as community radio is by far the most important medium for development and social change in rural communities.

subjective.question: Discuss the standards for community journalism.
subjective.answer: A community journalist is an integral member of a community of interest, and those engaged in it should be competent in carrying out their work to agreed standards. The main standards are: (1) Develop yourself as a journalist - keep up to date with developments in journalism, seek training opportunities, and understand the organization you work for and your role within it. (2) Develop ideas for stories - discuss issues with colleagues, keep up to date with local news and affairs, identify issues affecting the community, and develop ways of investigating issues of community concern. (3) Plan and carry out community assignments - agree objectives and deadlines, clarify resources and roles, attend on time with the right equipment, and complete assignments within agreed times and resources. (4) Cover community events - obtain information about events, cover predictable 'diary' events and unpredictable 'off-diary' events such as accidents and emergencies, and interview people about their attitudes towards events. (5) Produce copy - collect accurate information from a range of sources, check its accuracy, present it appropriately, and meet deadlines and house style.

subjective.question: What is needed to be followed for planning and carrying out community assignments?
subjective.answer: For planning and carrying out community assignments, the journalist must: agree the objectives and deadlines of assignments; clarify the resources available to carry out the assignment; clarify tasks and roles for different parts of the assignment; recognize health and safety hazards and take appropriate action to control risks; attend at the agreed time and place with the equipment needed; dress appropriately and conduct oneself in a proper manner; complete the assignment within agreed times and resources; complete records and reports relevant to the assignment; and identify ways in which work can be improved in future.

subjective.topic: Status of Women in a Local Community
subjective.question: Describe the status of women in Pakistan with reference to the 1998 census data.
subjective.answer: Women form 48 percent of the total population of Pakistan. According to the 1998 census data, 88 million people live in rural areas and 42 million in urban areas, and 45 percent of the population is below 15 years of age. The average age of women for marriage increased from 17.9 years in 1951 to 20.8 years in 1981. The majority of women are married to their close relatives (first or second cousins); only 37 percent are not related to their spouses before marriage. The divorce rate is extremely low, and most divorces occur in the lower income groups of urban areas. Women-headed households constituted 7 percent of total households in 1996-97. The overall literacy rate is only 45 percent - 56.5 percent for men and 32.6 percent for women - and the literacy rate for rural women is as low as 20.8 percent. Girls' primary school enrolment was 66.6 percent against 90.7 percent for boys, and the girls' dropout rate at primary level is 50 percent.

subjective.question: Discuss violence against women in Pakistan: its forms and extent.
subjective.answer: Violence is the most powerful mechanism used by family, society and state to silence women's voices of resistance to the existing gender-related social order. The study conducted by the Women's Division suggests that domestic violence takes place in approximately 80 percent of households in the country. The most commonly reported forms of violence are murder, stove burning, acid throwing, rape, abduction, forced marriage and honour crimes. During 1998, 282 burn cases were reported in Punjab and 65 percent of the victims died of their injuries; the official figure for murder of women during 1998 was 1,974; and according to official statistics one woman is raped every six hours. Of the 706 rape cases reported in Punjab in 1998, 55 percent of the victims were minors. Victims face further barriers: the Hudood Ordinance requires four witnesses for a rape charge, there are only 13 state-run darul-amans (shelters) in the country, and there is no legislation on domestic violence.

subjective.topic: Status of Children in a Local Community
subjective.question: Discuss the status of children in Pakistan and the problems they face.
subjective.answer: Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Pakistan signed and ratified in 1990, a child is any person under the age of 18. However, in Pakistan there is no agreed definition of the child: a child can be jailed at the age of 7, can enter the labour market at 14, boys can be married at 18 and girls at 16, and a child becomes an adult citizen at 21. Of 40 million children, 3.3 million were found to be economically active on a full-time basis, and the incidence of child labour is very high in carpet weaving, surgical instruments, sports goods, brick kilns and agriculture. Children are exposed to physical and sexual abuse at workplaces and within the home, and the law is silent on domestic violence. The National Commission for Child Welfare and Development (NCCWD) is the nucleus body dealing with child rights, but it is a commission without statutory powers.

subjective.question: Discuss the major education issues in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: Education in Pakistan is in a critical state. Pakistan is one of only 12 countries in the world that spends less than 2 percent of its GDP on education, and the UNDP Human Development Report gives it the lowest 'education index' score for any country outside Africa. According to the First Education Census 2006, there are about 25 million children not going to school and approximately 10 million children engaged in child labour. Pakistan has about 6.463 million out-of-school children of primary school age, the second largest number in any country in the world. Girls account for 57 percent of all out-of-school children worldwide (2004), and within Pakistan rural girls and women are the most disadvantaged. Successive governments have failed to deliver on their commitments, including the Education for All target of universal primary education.

subjective.question: Describe the composition of minorities in Pakistan and the problems they face.
subjective.answer: According to the 1981 census (total population 84,253,644), the minorities of Pakistan included Christians (1,310,426), Hindus (1,276,116), Ahmadis (104,244), Parsis (7,007), Buddhists (2,639) and Sikhs (2,146); overall, minorities represent about 8 percent of the total population, and by the 1998 census their number was nearing 11 to 13 million. Christians are divided roughly equally between Catholics and Protestants, and a large number of them are very poor and engaged in sanitary work, agriculture and domestic labour. Distinct small communities include the Kalasha of Chitral, who number around 3,000 and live in three small, land-locked hamlets. The problems faced by minorities include poverty, low literacy, occupational segregation into menial jobs, and social and economic marginalization.

subjective.question: What is development news? Discuss the objectives of development news reporting.
subjective.answer: According to John V. Vilanilam, development news relates to the primary, secondary and tertiary needs of a developing country. Primary needs are food, clothing and shelter; secondary needs are agricultural production, industrial production and social and cultural development; tertiary needs are infrastructure, energy, water management, transport, communication and conservation. Development, as defined by Aggrawala (1978), is a widely participatory process of directed social change in a society, intended to bring about both social and material advancement, including greater equality, freedom and other valued qualities, for the majority of the people through their gaining greater control over their environment. The objectives of development news reporting are: to give voice to the people; to inform the people about development activities; to strengthen the democratic process; and to critically evaluate the difference between the planned scheme and its actual implementation. Community journalism can be called a branch of development journalism.

subjective.question: What is community engagement? Explain the Six 'C's of successful community engagement.
subjective.answer: Community engagement is a broad term for connecting with a particular group of people; in relation to government, Cavaye defines it as the mutual communication and deliberation that occurs between government and citizens. Engagement should encourage an informed community voice and sustained two-way communication, and it should be open, honest, inclusive, respectful, committed and willing to collaborate. Brown and Isaacs have identified six C's of successful community engagement: (1) Capability - community members develop the skills and confidence to participate. (2) Commitment - a shared willingness to engage and follow through. (3) Contribution - everyone has something to offer and is enabled to contribute. (4) Continuity - engagement is sustained over time, not a one-off event. (5) Collaboration - partners work together, sharing power and decisions. (6) Conscience - engagement is guided by ethical values and the common good.

subjective.question: How can attitudes be changed through mass communication?
subjective.answer: Attitudes are inferred states of readiness to react in an evaluative way, in support of or against a given stimulus situation; they are learned, and they can be changed by mass communication, as more than one hundred studies have shown. To accomplish attitude change, a suggestion for change must first be received and accepted; as intelligence is the critical factor in the learning of factual material, acceptance is the critical factor in the learning of attitudes. People tend to avoid communication unsympathetic to their existing attitudes, or forget it, or recast it to fit their existing frame of reference. A suggestion is more likely to be accepted if it meets existing personality needs and drives. It is also possible, through preparatory communication, to build resistance to later contrary messages, which is why the attitude structure of children is more flexible than that of adults.
